title: Short Stuff: Fanta - Nazi Favorite?
summary: Short Stuff episode examining whether Fanta is a "Nazi drink." The hosts open with casual banter about their personal soda habits (Fanta orange, Tab, Mountain Dew, Mellow Yellow). They then trace Coca-Cola's history from its 1886 invention by John Stith Pemberton, through its expansion into Germany under Max Keith (spelled "Kite" in the transcript) and Coca-Cola GmbH, its ties to the Nazi era including the 1936 Berlin Olympics sponsorship, and the wartime syrup cutoff that led Keith to create Fanta from leftover ingredients (apple pulp, beet sugar, whey). They discuss the drink's post-war reformulation and 1955 relaunch, its introduction in Italy and US arrival in 1958, the name's German meaning (fantasy), and Keith's later rise to head of Coca-Cola Europe. Source for much of the history is Mark Pendergrast's book.

segments.title: Opening banter about Fanta and soda habits
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the Fanta slogan and share personal soda preferences, including Chuck's fondness for Fanta orange and Josh's childhood taste for Fago. They mention Tab, Mountain Dew and Mellow Yellow.

segments.title: Coca-Cola origins and expansion into Germany
segments.summary: Chuck recounts John Stith Pemberton's 1886 invention of Coca-Cola. Josh describes the company's global expansion and its German subsidiary, Coca-Cola GmbH, led by Max Keith, by the late 1930s.

segments.title: Keith's Nazi ties and the 1936 Olympics banners
segments.summary: Citing Mark Pendergrast's book, the hosts say Keith wove Coca-Cola into German life and worked closely with the Nazi Party though he reportedly never officially joined. Coca-Cola co-sponsored the 1936 Berlin Olympics with banners beside the swastika. Josh describes a 1939 mass salute at the subsidiary's tenth anniversary to celebrate Hitler's birthday.

segments.title: Wartime seizure and loss of Coke syrup
segments.summary: When the war began, Coca-Cola stopped supplying its secret syrup to Germany, and the German government seized enemy-owned businesses, which hurt the German subsidiary. Keith needed a new product.

segments.title: Creation of Fanta from wartime leftovers
segments.summary: Keith created Fanta from leftovers due to sugar rationing and the loss of Coke syrup. The hosts describe the ingredients (apple pulp, beet sugar, whey), the name's meaning as German for fantasy or imagination, and the drink's poor taste, with it likely sold as a flavoring for soups and stews.

segments.title: Fanta's popularity in wartime Germany
segments.summary: Despite the poor taste, Fanta sold well in Germany and became a point of national pride among Germans for resourcefulness during scarcity.

segments.title: Post-war reformulation, Italy launch, and the name debate
segments.summary: Keith's ties to the Nazi Party were a matter of necessity to keep production running. Coca-Cola reformulated Fanta in 1955 and kept the name. The drink launched in Italy first and reached the US in 1958. The hosts debate whether the name was tainted outside Germany.

segments.title: Whether drinking Fanta supports Nazis and Keith's later career
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether buying Fanta today supports Nazis, with Pendergrast's view that people still enjoy it for what it is. Keith was later made head of Coca-Cola Europe, and Josh notes his consolidation of European businesses under the Nazi conquests.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh asks whether Chuck wants a Fanta and the hosts close the episode. Chuck gives the iHeartRadio production credit.
